title: 100% procedural UI in Godot, zero textures or sprites, just Godot AI
author: d-czar
selftext:
I wanted to share a set of interactive UI panels I built in Godot using zero art assets. They're all drawn with Godot custom\_draw() calls like`draw_polyline,draw_polygon`,`draw_arc, etc.`Godot 4.6, no shaders, no sprites, no textures at all.

I know it's not triple A or triple I or whatever, but I thought it was not bad for a couple hours of fun experimenting. I used an open source plugin I've been building called Godot AI. (I'm the lead contributor to the 8,500 GitHub star MCP for Unity, and I thought it'd be good to bring AI/MCP lessons learned there to the Godot community. :)

comments.author: SuperHornetFA18
comments.body: This is amazing ! what was your train of thought when you started building this ?

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: I mainly wanted to test out the capabilities of the Godot AI / MCP tool I've been building.  It does a bunch of stuff that makes operating in the editor a lot faster.  But I spent some time building a toolset for it that lets it programatically draw cool UI and effects without needing to generate any images.  Godot AI also does a bunch of other stuff (materials, node setup, scene management, takes screenshots to give back to your LLM to tell it how it's doing).  Free and open source if you wanna try it -- [https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai](https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai)

comments.author: insats
comments.body:
What exactly is it that your tool does? It’s already possible and simply to use agentic coding with Godot, and there’s an MCP for Godot which lets the agent launch scenes etc when needed. 

I’m also not sure what’s so impressive here. Godot is basically a rendering and animation engine, and drawing this UI is nothing miraculous, it’s completely natural. You could do the same in Skia, and probably also with HTML canvas for that matter.

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body:
I appreciate and understand your skepticism. Every other post is about a cool new tool these days. 

I’ve spent a year building the MCP for Unity, which hundreds of thousands of people have used, and learned a lot both from building it and listening to the community, about what makes a good MCP/CLI suite for game dev.  My goal for this one is not to have 500 tools, but to select and develop a set of robust and useful tools that hit the biggest pain points.  That’s easy scene and node querying and configuration, automated screenshots to feed back to the agent, multiple editor sessions sharing one MCP server, strong flexible UI design, materials, particles and shaders. Most of that is already in there and been smoke tested to high heaven to give people (and LLMs) a smooth experience. 

In the case of the UI example here, rule absolutely right the primitives are all there in godot. But picking which ones to bundle together into reusable tools helps make AI-assisted gamedev faster, so agents don’t have to figure out the right editor API calls every time from scratch.   

I can only say, please give it a try, and if you think it’s not useful, I’ll certainly respect that. But I would also be surprised!   Thanks for the question.

replies.author: Lunettes-oo
replies.body: Do you think that would be possible for someone with very little knowledge in programming to « vibe code » a full on deckbuilding coop game like slay the spire 2 for example ?

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body:
Yes and No.  The Yes part is that it's technically possible, the coding part is kind of optional at this point -- the AI models plus tools like Godot AI can do like 99% of the coding for you.  But there are still things you have to learn, know, and understand to build any kind of sophisticated game.  Why? Because you need to guide the AI as it builds, correct it, test what it does, give it feedback, tell it what to build.  

So the yes part is if you put in the work and research and hours to learn what the pieces are of a game like that, it's definitely possible with very little coding.  But the no part is, learning the pieces is a big investment of time to learn.  So it depends on how much you're willing to put into it -- but it's way more possible than it used to be!

replies.author: Lunettes-oo
replies.body: Thanks for your time that’s a very great answer

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: Sure thing --- I added the second pargraph with the "flame" example that I think helps explain the challenge a bit better.

replies.author: Lunettes-oo
replies.body: Alright, so the hard part might actually be the visuals, animations and assets. But if you stand on a very minimalist approach, very simple visuals etc… Godot AI can already do this?

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body:
I would say basically yes.  And that's probably a good place to start if you're just starting out.  Define what the absolute minimum version of this would be, even with a few cards/powers and a couple enemies. That alone would be a good amount of work -- but trying to do will be less overwhelming than trying to build a whole giant game from scratch if it's your first time.  So yeah, you can even work with the AI and say, hey, I Want to do a deckbuilder in Godot, but it's my first time doing this -- how can we start small and build a little prototype? Which elements do we need? Let's make a plan."  

Then you'll learn about what the pieces are and it'll start to make sense

replies.author: Lunettes-oo
replies.body: So if I have for example already defined 4 classes of character with a list of 300 cards I can give that to Godot AI. Will it creates the visuals of the cards on its own if I give specific orders for each card ? Or do the visuals have to be done externally, that’s why your thread took my attention. Your UI is very polished

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: You could use these tools to do some basic card templales -- say a card background with the name of the card, and "cost" and damage and mana points and stuff like that. But you'd probably still want image art for the main image on the card, even if it's a small image in a circle.  But depends how you did it -- you could have Godot try to draw little cyberpunky-symbol/icons for the cards to, using the above tools.  Lots of ways to do it

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body:
It can create and alter materials, particles, do sophisticated UI, intelligently take screenshots from editor viewport and game view so LLM can see what it’s doing, write and attach scripts, read console logs, set up audio and animation tracks, and other things.  The best way to find out is to give it a try, it takes 5 minutes to set up. Info is all here.

https://github.com/hi-godot/godot-ai

Remember to Die is a great name! It looks cool too.  My tip for the UI is to find a few references you like, give it to the LLM (with Godot AI) and say, make a plan to give me a v2 of my console in this style, and have it do v2 in a new scene alongside the old scene (instead of overwriting v1), so you have the evolution.  Then work with it to iterate the fine details — glow, gradient, border, animations. For the example above, I think I did like up to v3.2 or something.  And I would give it more references and say like now add angular corners like these, etc.  Some was overkill obviously but I wanted to just keep pushing it and it kept getting better, and it was fun.  Let me know if it works for you!

replies.author: d-czar
replies.body: Absolutely, that’s literally the most useful thing about it, is giving the LLMs much more flexible and deep access to the data architecture of your game.  As for whether they could “play”, you’d have to probably set up some scripts or triggers so could “advance” through the game.  Actually playing with human reflexes and mouse / stick moving would be harder but not impossible with AI “computer use” tools.
